source.title: Real Time Detection and Quantitative Analysis of Spurious Forgetting in Continual Learning

record.tranche_reason: Builds a continual-learning framework around shallow alignment and spurious forgetting, then reports its own training and mitigation results. It does not test safety refusals or the safety-specific mechanisms in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper studies task alignment and forgetting on classification tasks, not safety-trained chat models, harmful prompts, refusal rates, harmful-prompt KL, compliant prefills, suffix attacks, decoding changes, or safety-related parameters. The task-alignment results below are related but different constructs, so they are recorded as none and do not support verdicts on the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The paper borrows the 'shallow alignment' framing (alignment concentrated in the first 3-5 tokens) and applies it to task alignment in continual learning on classification datasets (CLINC-150, 20 Newsgroups). It measures a cosine-similarity 'alignment depth' and task forgetting rates, not harmful compliance, refusal, per-token KL on harmful prompts, prefill or suffix attacks, or safety parameters. It does not use the safety finding as a tool either. Its claims about 'fine-tuning attacks' are asserted, not measured. This is a related but different construct, so it is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that task alignment in continual learning is only a few tokens deep (D≤3 under standard training) and that this explains spurious forgetting. Their deep-alignment training (D>12) and adaptive mitigation cut forgetting and beat fixed freezing by 3.3-7.1%. They also assert, without testing, that shallowness explains why fine-tuning attacks work.
record.recipe_differences: Studies continual learning on classification datasets and introduces task-alignment metrics and training strategies; it does not use the safety fine-tuning, harmful-prompt KL, or compliant-prefill methods in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports sensitivity to alignment/reversibility thresholds and monitoring frequency in Table 14, but does not report these as changes to safety behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: In continual learning on classification tasks across four Qwen models, a position-weighted 'deep alignment' training raises the cosine-based task-alignment depth from about 3 to 12-14. It also cuts task forgetting from 11-12.5% to 2.2-3.1%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task-alignment depth across token positions is shallow under standard continual-learning training and can be deepened to reduce task forgetting.

record.problems: The reported alignment-depth and forgetting-rate values in Table 6 have no uncertainty estimates there. The study evaluates task classification and task forgetting, so its results do not establish safety behavior.
record.rows_left_out: Detection accuracy, recovery time, robustness scores, and mitigation comparisons were not recorded because they concern the paper's forgetting-detection framework rather than the claim's safety behavior or token-position alignment measure.

untested.parts: All: no harmful fine-tuning, no harmful-compliance measure.
All: no harmful-compliance measure after benign training.
All: no per-token KL between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
All: no prefill, suffix or decoding attacks on refusal.
All for safety. A gradient-decay argument is given for task alignment only, without safety data.
All for safety. Its 'deep alignment training' targets task forgetting, not refusal robustness.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from uses_without_test/T4 to discusses/T6. The paper does not rely on the safety finding as a tool. It borrows the terminology and analogizes it to a different construct. Its alignment score is a cosine between hidden states times output weights and labels. The numbers are suspiciously regular, and the models are run via Ollama while fine-tuning is claimed. Treat with caution.

versions.untested_parts: Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Compliant prefills, adversarial suffixes, decoding changes, and harmful completion rates.
Whether safety behavior is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether safety-training data or objectives cause shallow safety behavior.
Whether safety training can deepen safety behavior and whether that safety behavior remains robust.

relation.reason: The abstract and discussion connect shallow alignment to fine-tuning attacks, but provide no safety measurements or tests of that assertion.

tranche.reason: The experiments measure classification-task alignment and forgetting, not any safety claim version. The paper does not operationally use an established safety-alignment finding.

source_check.notes: All rows accurately reproduce Table 6 but concern task metrics; the own-method comparisons should not count as phenomenon evidence. The paper's repeated standard-training summary D≤3 conflicts with Table 6 values 3.1 and 3.2.
